# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why1: At the last step before strangers see the study, deciding whether to collect emails from people who say yes is exactly the right moment, and for me it is the bridge to the 15-day risk-free order.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is plain YC-batch language to me, and the hint spells out exactly what the respondent will see and where I find the answers.
screens.why3: It is my own call about my own launch, and I know I want names of deaf and hard-of-hearing adults willing to wear the glasses.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it cleanly, with no overlap and nothing missing for a simple opt-in.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is reworded, and the respondent line 'Would you try this for real?' leaks no product name or role.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is the obvious last step before the link goes out, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question is clear, but it misspells my own people as 'aduts', and the hint packs voice, video, credits and text delivery into one paragraph, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: I can judge which voice my deaf and hard-of-hearing wearers would be comfortable with, since I know how they meet a talking face.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices are fine, but for respondents who mostly can't hear there is no text-only or captioned-first option, which is the choice I would most want.
screens.why5: My actor is kept but misspelled, and a voice-first interviewer drifts a little from the fact that many of my respondents will read rather than listen.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Options: Daphne (on-screen text with voice) · Saskia (on-screen text with voice) · Text on screen only, no voice

screens.why1: Once I've picked who asks the questions, choosing how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: The choice is clear to me, but 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' makes me stop and work out that it means Daphne's voice is still being made.
screens.why3: I know my users and can judge on the spot whether a talking video interviewer or a read-and-tap page suits deaf and hard-of-hearing adults.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete, but the Daphne option is written for hearing people ('asks each question aloud', 'Hear her', speech caught 9 in 10 times where it is loud) and says nothing about how well she catches deaf speech, which is the part that matters for my respondents.
screens.why5: It names my respondents in my own words and leaks nothing about AirCaps or the glasses.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? — Read and tap (each question written, they tap or type; ready now) / AI interviewer Daphne (every question captioned on screen, they can sign-free type, tap or talk; ready in a few minutes) / Let them choose when they open the link

screens.why1: After choosing who interviews and how people answer, deciding who receives the link is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words for a founder; 'link', 'Contacts page' and 'signs in with Google' are ordinary to someone who has just used Keel.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching hard-of-hearing people I know personally, a found list, or a community group like an HLAA chapter or a Facebook group.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, but the option labels and descriptions run together without punctuation ('People I know by name I send each one...'), and a group of deaf adults may balk at a mandatory Google sign-in with no alternative mentioned.
screens.why5: Nothing of my idea is altered; it simply routes the study I built.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (I send each their own link) / A list I found with Keel (Keel makes a link per person; I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already gather, e.g. an HLAA chapter or online group)

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right under the title, and "3 holding" plus each card's "7 of 7 · bar 5 of 7" give the numbers that decide it.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on this page, but each card says what was counted, over 7 people, against a bar of 5 of 7, so it reads at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The three card names and belief lines are exactly what I checked, but the solution statement under the title is garbled ("the adult the app on lightweight glasses shows... and gets back live captions...") and is not a sentence I would sign.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what three holding cards mean for AirCaps or what to do next; "What it measures" only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible, but unanimous 7 of 7 is called "Holding up" with no note that seven people is a small read, and the 3 conditional adopters only show up as a trailing aside.
screens.instead: Say "All 3 checks held with 7 people: every one would have followed more and would wear them, though 3 only on a condition, so read those conditions before you price," and fix the solution sentence to: "When a conversation is too fast or noisy, the wearer reads live captions of nearby speech inside the lens."

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right above "7 of 7 said yes or yes, with some steps · bar 5 of 7", so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: Yes 4 and with-some-steps 3 for, No 0 against, over 7 people with the marker at 5. The second bar wording, "no more than 1 in 3 say no", is redundant but doesn't confuse.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Compatibility and uses my belief line word for word: their phone was with them and online.
screens.why_b4: The So line points me to adoption friction, but it never says what the "some steps" were for 3 of my 7. The three quotes tagged Compatibility are about trying a demo pair or hearing audience questions, not about the phone, so I can't tell whether pairing is a hidden hurdle.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says "a small group: a lean, not a call". The So line still flatly says the phone "is not what will stop them" and names adoption friction as the blocker, which is more than 7 people can carry on one screen.
screens.instead: 7 of 7 had their phone with them and online, 3 only after some steps (say which: pairing, data, battery). With 7 people that's a lean, not a call; the try-before-you-buy notes here belong under adoption friction.

screens.why_b1: The card says Holding up with 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7 directly beside it, so I know my belief held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts 'better' answers, 7 a lot and 0 a little, over the 7 who answered, and the marker at 5 of 7 shows at once that I cleared the bar.
screens.why_b3: The title is the Relative advantage I checked, and the belief line, 'following more without asking anyone to repeat', is word for word what I confirmed on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates that all 7 imagined it going better and points me on to Adoption friction, but it never says what a unanimous 'a lot better' means for me, such as leading with that benefit.
screens.why_b5: n stays at 7, the count line says it is a small group and a lean, not a call, and it flags that the answer is a hypothetical about their last conversation, so the 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: All 7 imagined their last conversation going a lot better, but it is a hypothetical lean from 7 people: lead with 'no more asking people to repeat', then see under Adoption friction whether they would actually wear the glasses.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 3 on a condition", so I know it held and by how much over my bar.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, 4 yes and 3 yes-if-worth-it for me, none against, and the marker at 5 of 7 is plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: "Adoption friction" and "Most would wear the glasses, paired to the phone" are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line promises that what would make it worth it to the 3 conditional yeses is below, but all that's there is Tomás's end-seat quote, which explains his workaround rather than what would tip him, so I still don't know what to fix or prove for those three.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, "a small group: a lean, not a call" is said, and the 3 conditional yeses are split out rather than folded silently into 7 of 7.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 would wear them as is; 3 only if clearly worth it. Tomás already gets by with the end seat, so for the conditional ones show the noisy-table moment where the workaround fails.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on 'Holding up' with '7 of 7 … bar 5 of 7' right beside it, and the lead-in repeats 'held, 7 of 7', so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b3: Both belief lines, 'phone was with them and online' and 'would wear the glasses, paired to the phone', are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do: the screen never turns 'try a demo pair first' or 'borrow one for a matinee' into a next step such as a loaner or demo programme, or a test of mic pickup for audience questions, and Relative advantage has no box at all.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible, but '2 never saw it (Harriet, Ruth)' reads as if they skipped adoption when they answered on Compatibility, and '3 on a condition' sits over only one quote, so the conditional yeses look firmer than they are.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me things I did not type: people want to try before buying (a noisy walk while moving, reading the lens under stage lights), the mics need to pick up audience questions, and one-side-deaf users like Tomás already have an end-seat workaround that 'works most of the time', which is a real competing habit.
screens.instead: Compatibility and adoption held 7 of 7, but most yeses hang on trying a pair first (walk, matinee, big hall), so offer a demo or loaner and test mic pickup beyond the front speaker; one-side-deaf users already manage with seating, so they are a weaker wedge.

screens.why1: Opening by asking whether I talk with hearing people every week is a sensible gate, since that is who the study is about.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is exactly how I and other deaf people say it, and the question is short and clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I talk with hearing people in a week: at work, at the shops, with family.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate like this, the two can't overlap, and leaving out an escape is right for a screener.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment, talking with hearing people every week, without saying anything about a product or using any label I wouldn't use myself.
screens.why6: It is short and easy to follow, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is stiff for a yes-or-no, and the guidelines' own screener form would just say 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Do you talk with hearing people every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Narrowing from 'every week' to the last 7 days makes sense before asking for the story, but it nearly repeats the screen I just answered.
screens.why2: 'Follow and join' is two things in one: I'm in conversations every week, but I often can't follow them and only half join in, so I don't know whether to say yes or no.
screens.why3: I was in face-to-face conversations this week, but whether I 'followed and joined' them is a judgement I'd have to guess at, because that's exactly what goes wrong for me.
screens.why4: My truest answer, 'I was there but couldn't really follow', is missing, and the gate carries two escape chips, including 'I'd rather not say', where a gate should have none.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's job phrase word for word, but 'follow and join a face-to-face conversation' is the founder's wording, not how I'd ever put it.
screens.why6: It's short with a clear 'Yes or no.', but 'follow and join' is two questions in one breath when heard.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, were you in a face-to-face conversation with hearing people? Yes / No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: After asking whether I talked with hearing people this week, showing me the idea before the idea questions makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Most of it is plain, but 'glasses with the app on them' made me stop, because nothing before it said AirCaps was an app, and I wondered if it runs on my phone or in the glasses.
screens.why3: Reading captions while still looking at the person is exactly what I miss at a noisy table or a fast meeting, so I can picture it in my own week.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options, chips or value box.
screens.why5: The idea is shown on purpose and plainly, and nothing reads like the company's own jargon about people like me.
screens.why6: It is short, plain sentences with no symbols or brackets, easy to take in once, whether I hear it or read the captions.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, live captions inside your glasses. You wear light glasses, and the words people nearby are saying show up inside the lens as they talk. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the glasses idea, it makes sense to ask whether my phone was with me and online, since I'd guess the glasses need it.
screens.why2: The question drops its subject and verb, so 'Have your phone with you and online?' reads like a fragment and I had to read it twice to see it means 'Did you have your phone with you, and was it online?'.
screens.why3: I know whether my phone was in my pocket with signal at my last conversation, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No fit, but 'Yes, with some steps' is odd for having a phone on me; it's either there and online or not, so the middle option has no clear meaning here.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's name and what it does reach me, which is shown on purpose, and nothing of the founder's own terms leaks.
screens.why6: It is short with three options I can hold, but the clipped 'Have your phone with you and online?' sounds broken when said aloud and could leave me unsure what is being asked.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation. Did you have your phone with you, with signal or Wi-Fi? Yes; yes, but it took some fixing; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: It follows on from my answer about having my phone with me and online, but it jumps straight in without saying which steps it means, so it lands a bit abruptly.
screens.why2: I'd have to stop and work out what "it" is: getting my phone online, or the conversation itself.
screens.why3: I know what I do to get my phone ready, like turning on data or finding the wifi and opening my captioning app, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing about anyone's product or plan comes through; it just asks what I did.
screens.why6: Five short words and one question, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: What did you have to do to get your phone ready and online for that conversation?

screens.why1: Right after the card about captions in glasses, it makes sense to ask whether they would have helped in the conversation I just thought about.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself, although 'go better' could mean following people or getting a word in, and I'd take it as both.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last chat went and where I lost the thread, so I can judge whether captions in front of my eyes would have helped.
screens.why4: The four choices cover it, including 'Worse', which is real for me if reading the captions pulled my eyes off people's faces and lips, and 'I can't tell' fits if I've never worn anything like that.
screens.why5: It only uses the name and the idea from the card, says 'conversation' the way I would, and doesn't push any other product talk on me.
screens.why6: One short question with four short choices said as a list, then the one escape, easy to take in at once, though for me it would be the on-screen text I'd follow.

screens.why1: Straight after asking whether AirCaps would have helped my last conversation, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually put the glasses on and keep my phone paired to use it.
screens.why2: Glasses, phone and paired are everyday words to me since my hearing aids pair to my phone too, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I'd wear captioning glasses out with hearing people is my own call about my own face and my own day, so I can answer it from what I know.
screens.why4: The four options cover the range, but many of us already wear prescription glasses, and my true answer is 'only if they take my lenses', which only loosely fits under 'if it was clearly worth it'.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea card's plain meaning of captions in glasses worn with a phone, and no founder terms or plans leak through.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold, and a single escape said last.
screens.instead: To use AirCaps, you'd wear the glasses paired to your phone. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Yes, if they took my prescription · Yes, if it was clearly worth it · Probably not · No; escape: I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I'd wear the glasses with my phone, it makes sense to ask what would tip it for me.
screens.why2: Short, everyday words; I'd get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know what I'd need: captions that keep up in a noisy pub, catch who's talking, and don't make me look odd at the table.
screens.why4: Just a box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was introduced on the idea card, so naming it here isn't a leak, and nothing of the founder's own terms comes through.
screens.why6: One short question with no list or symbols, easy to hear once and answer.
